messages.body_plain:
Hello,

My apologies if I failed to find a similar archive post.

My study involves one year of bird point count sampling over three repeat visits with distance recorded. I would like to determine density using distance estimation at 42 different sites using a global detection function. The global detection function is necessary, because most of my sites are small fragments where it is impossible to increase sampling intensity.

I selected gdistsamp, because I also wanted to estimate phi and ran the model using site as a covariate with 42 levels. However, the model fails to converge, which doesn't really surprise me given the large number of covariate levels.

Warning message:
In gdistsamp(~site, ~site, ~1, dist.myco1, output = "density"  :
  Hessian is singular. Try using fewer covariates and supplying starting values.

I have tried various models that use starting data from a simpler model and changing K - all fail to converge. Likewise, I've been unable to find a different approach in the archives here or in other published resources.

Many thanks for your help.

Best,
Ian Ausprey

Estimating a separate density for each site is kind of like estimating a separate intercept for every datum within a standard regression analysis--hence the error. It sounds like maybe you are more interested in the realized density than the expected density? If so, calls to ranef/bup (see ?ranef) after a model has been fit might get you what you need.

John

I think you would have to go a Bayesian route to get site-specific phi estimates (lacking any covariates, treating site-specific phi as a random effect). Uncharacteristically high density estimates using gdistsamp has to be one of the most common questions on the board: density in this model relates to lambda(or N) and phi. Consider something like

library(boot)
inv.logit(coef(m1)[2])*bup(ranef(m1))

rather than

bup(ranef(m1))

John

The issue ultimately is that I am trying to combine methods from distance estimation and occupancy modeling to understand how detection probability is governed by two components: (1) how well I am able to detect a vocalizing individual (ie., interspecific variation in effective distance radius) and (2) whether or not a bird is available to detect during a given sampling period (ie., it doesn't vocalization or it's not there).

Hence, the issue with gdistsamp (as I understand it) is that phi is a global estimate while the realized estimates of lambda are site specific. There might be some trick to do so but it appears that when using pcountOpen the choices are (1) setting all recruitment rates to zero (using the option fix="gamma") or (2) allowing that recruitment rate between period 2 and 3 to be estimated and test to see if that is zero.

The more direct way is to construct the likelihood function with that recruitment rate set to zero.  If your proposed set of models are not too complicated (and the data is "nice"), then writing code to duplicate pcountOpen for those models is certainly possible.  To state the obvious there's a lot of quality assurance resulting in stability of the pcountOpen code which would not necessarily be the case for any home-grown versions.  But if such a model is desired, then that's what you'd likely need to do.

So....how complicated are the models you're considering?

Jim

Hi All,

I'm trying to run multiseason occupancy models to assess the influence of altitude on the colonisation and extinction rates of multiple butterfly species in a Spanish mountain range, however I'm having trouble getting my models to run when using both altitude and altitude squared as my covariates.

Initially I was standardising my data for altitude to bring it closer to 0 (originally this variable ranged from ~800 to 2400), when standardising altitude my models were running fine, however I was advised that standardising this variable makes the coefficients uninterpretable.

I've attached a copy of the data that I'm using for one of the species (Hesperia comma) and below is my code:

library(unmarked)

data <- read.csv("Hcomma.csv")

y <- data[,3:12]

#Creating yearly site covariates

year <- as.character(c(2004,2017))

year<- matrix(year, nrow(data),2,byrow = TRUE)

year.covs <- data.frame(
  year = matrix(t(year),ncol = 1)
)

#Creating observational covariates

season    <- data[,15:24]

obs.cov   <-data.frame(season = matrix(t(season),ncol=1))

# Creating site covariates

site.cov <- data.frame(Alt = data[,13], AltSq = data[,14])

#Creating an unmarked frame

comma <- unmarkedMultFrame(
  y=y,
  yearlySiteCovs = year.covs,
  obsCovs = obs.cov,
  siteCovs = site.cov,
  numPrimary = 2
)

# fitting models

fm1<-colext( ~1,  ~1,  ~1, ~1, data=comma)

fm2<-colext( ~1, ~1, ~1, ~season, data=comma)

fm4<-colext( ~1, ~Alt, ~1, ~1, data=comma)

fm5<-colext( ~1, ~1, ~Alt, ~1, data=comma)

fm6<-colext( ~Alt, ~1, ~1, ~1, data=comma)

fm7 <-colext( ~Alt, ~Alt, ~Alt, ~1, data=comma) - These initial models above including just altitude run fine.

fm8<-colext( ~Alt+AltSq, ~Alt, ~Alt, ~1, data=comma) - However, as soon as I introduce AltSq, I get the following error code:

> fm8<-colext( ~Alt+AltSq, ~Alt, ~Alt, ~1, data=comma)
Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = getHessian, ...) :
  non-finite finite-difference value [3]

I've had a good read through examples online and threads on this group but can't seem to find an answer, I've tried specifying a 'starts' value, however this hasn't worked unfortunately.

Any help would be much appreciated, it may be something very simple, I'm very new to both R and Unmarked, my apologies!

Thanks very much,

Lee.

"...however I was advised that standardising this variable makes the coefficients uninterpretable."  Nonsense for at least three reasons: (1) one can always transform back, (2) I think there are very few folks that can appropriately "interpret" coefficients on a logistic scale even when the original units are used, and (3) Squaring numbers in the thousands (or even the hundreds such as the year 2018) usually results in lots of round-off error which in turn produces error messages such as the one you see.

But one doesn't have to "standardize" by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.  When one has elevation in feet or meters, dividing by 1,000 usually does the trick and makes it much easier to transform back.  (When one has the years 2003 through 2016, subtracting 2000 is probably all you need to do.)

 So changing the following lines of code from

> # Creating site covariates
> site.cov <- data.frame(Alt = data[,13], AltSq = data[,14])

to
> # Creating site covariates
> site.cov <- data.frame(Alt = data[,13]/1000, AltSq = (data[,13]/1000)^2)
>
will remove the error messages.

But that results in getting lots of NaN's for the standard errors for the colonization and extinction parameter estimates which is a different issue.  (I'll look at that later today but that should NOT stop anyone else from looking into why that is happening.)

Jim

Dear Jim,

excellent remarks ! We transform covariates way too often in ways that makes interpretation of the coefficients really hard, e.g. by normalizing them. Instead, as you say, we should much better strive to transform them such that they keep some useful interpretation, e.g., that an altitude is expressed in kms instead of metres or a date in months instead of days etc.

Best regards  --- Marc

"...however I was advised that standardising this variable makes the coefficients uninterpretable."  Nonsense for at least three reasons: (1) one can always transform back, (2) I think there are very few folks that can appropriately "interpret" coefficients on a logistic scale even when the original units are used, and (3) Squaring numbers in the thousands (or even the hundreds such as the year 2018) usually results in lots of round-off error which in turn produces error messages such as the one you see.

But one doesn't have to "standardize" by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.  When one has elevation in feet or meters, dividing by 1,000 usually does the trick and makes it much easier to transform back.  (When one has the years 2003 through 2016, subtracting 2000 is probably all you need to do.)

 So changing the following lines of code from

> # Creating site covariates
> site.cov <- data.frame(Alt = data[,13], AltSq = data[,14])

to
> # Creating site covariates
> site.cov <- data.frame(Alt = data[,13]/1000, AltSq = (data[,13]/1000)^2)
>
will remove the error messages.

But that results in getting lots of NaN's for the standard errors for the colonization and extinction parameter estimates which is a different issue.  (I'll look at that later today but that should NOT stop anyone else from looking into why that is happening.)

Jim

The predictions will be nearly identical either way - standardizing with centering or dividing by an appropriate constant (well, almost identical depending on round-off error, the relative tolerance setting, etc.) and I lean much more into selecting models based on the overall model fit rather than the statistical significance of the individual coefficients.

If this is a problem with many datasets and models, I wonder if a version using multiple precision arithmetic might eventually become necessary?

messages.body_plain:
Hi all – hopefully this is a suitable place to ask these questions

Based on this post

(https://groups.google.com/d/msg/unmarked/izJU61k9hKI/sBNr9I-tnWYJ)

I have been reading about the models described in Chandler and Royle 2013 and Ramsey 2015. Have there been any further developments of these models since 2013/2015? Have they been more thoroughly tested/validated? I have not yet found other papers that use or develop these models further; a few review papers that mention them but no real studies as far as I can find.

I’m also hoping to get some study design advice in two situations, one regarding coyotes in a very urban environment (the Bronx) and another with white-tailed deer in a suburban forest preserve. In both cases the C&R and/or Ramsey models are attractive to us in terms of adapting our current camera surveys to (attempt to) actually measure abundance. What scale is appropriate for these models, in terms of both population size and area? Also, how would one interpret the resulting activity centers when looking at social or herding animals?

Additionally, how do these models handle social or family-grouped species, where animals often are photographed in groups of 3 or more? As far as I can tell, the model does not discriminate between, eg, a single photograph/observation of 3 deer vs. 3 observations of a single deer. Seems to me then that an activity center in this situation would be an activity center for a group or family, not just one animal, and therefore density ought to be higher than what the model might produce. Or the model results should be interpreted as # of social groups, not number of individuals.

If you are curious for more detail on what we’re hoping to do:

1. The deer study is probably a simpler situation so I’ll start there. We have been using a camera trap-based method of estimating deer densities based on an updated version of this protocol (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wsb.64/abstract) to measure the impact of ongoing deer management. I’d like to try C&R’s model this year and, if possible, on our prior years’ datasets and compare the two methods.

The area we are looking at is approximately 5 sq. km and in the past we’ve used 20 or so cameras. I can up this to 30+ cameras now, if that would enable us to use C&R’s 2013 model to greater precision. This is much smaller than the simulated 15x15 grid used in the 2013 paper, but given the area we’re interested in, 30 cams would represent a grid of 300m, 30% of an assumed 0.3km2 home range for suburban wt deer. Is this (~3-5km2) an appropriate study area for these models, or is it too small?

messages.subject: Can you have too many surveys?
messages.subject_clean: Can you have too many surveys?
messages.body_plain:
I have a generic (and possibly silly) question about occupancy modeling: is there ever such a thing as "too many surveys"?

I'm asking because it seems that some of the emergent "big data" survey methods (e.g. automated acoustic monitoring, camera trapping) have the opportunity to be quite survey-rich compared to traditional field studies, where folks are often hurting for surveys.

In one of these "big data" automated contexts, you could have, say, a 30 day sampling period for a single season, and be automatically collecting data every day. You could lump that data into survey periods of your choice. Maybe you define a survey as a single day (in which case, you would have an encounter history of 30 zeroes and ones). Alternatively, maybe you define a survey period as three days (in which case, you would have an encounter history of 30 days/3 = 10 zeroes and ones). Whatever you choose, you'd want to make sure your survey periods meet assumptions about closure for the target species in question.

I guess what I'm wondering is, is there ever any caution against "too many surveys"? In the example above, we're surveying for the same total time regardless -- we're just making different decisions over how to chop up that sampling period into surveys. It seems to me that the 30-survey specification would be better than the 10-survey specification, but perhaps there's a point at which too many surveys could challenge convergence or result in other unexpected behavior.

The occupancy literature I've read is largely concerned with the problem of too few surveys, so I'm just wondering if anyone knows of any literature or practical guidelines around this!

Dear Cathleen,

I don't think this is a silly question at all.

I think that the main consideration in the context of occupancy models is closure as you say. If closure is not a problem, then possibly you get such a high, combined detection probability that you may forget about modeling the detection process and simply fit a logistic regression to the aggregated survey result instead (i.e., to the binary indicator for whether the species is ever detected or not).

On the other hand, in the possible case that you are interested in parameters of the detection model, you would of course not want to do this.

I am sure there are other considerations as well.

Best regards  --- Marc

Dear Jesse,

I don't know the method you're mentioning, but here are some comments about occupancy and comparing stuff:

- If you have two sites, and only two sites, you can't really estimate an occupancy probability. You need spatial reps for that. If you mean you have two sites and then within each of them multiple reps (e.g., point counts), then it's OK.
- if you do have reps and can therefore estimate occupancy, the best to compare occupancy between the two "sites" = regions would be to fit a model with species random effects and a fixed region effect. If this turns out to be "important" (used to say "significant"), then there's your answer.
- I just realize that this really belongs into the realm of multi-species occupancy models and hence a full, integrated analysis cannot be done in unmarked. messages.body_plain:
If you are interested in predicting abundance, then you want those predictions based only on the abundance predictors.  pcount (and other routines in unmarked) allow one to get estimates "free and clear" of the nuisance caused by less-than-perfect detection.  While the detection parameters certainly influence the observed counts, the predictions are about what one would observe if detection was perfect.  Now if the detection probabilities are low that that will generally increase the standard errors for the estimates of abundance and the associated parameters.  So there is an influence in that respect.

Sometimes one is also interested in the detection part of the model to ascertain what factors influence detection probabilities and what one might want to do when designing future surveys.

And I might likely be in the minority here but if PC1+PC2+PC3 means the first three principal components of some set of environmental variables, then unless you have a solid interpretation for each component, I'd avoid using those.  Performing manipulations on a large set of variables in complete isolation of what one wants to predict makes little sense to me.  Yes, the principal components are orthogonal to each other (by definition) but there's no reason to believe that the top 3 principal components will be good predictors or better than any of the remaining principal components.

Jim
